props.title: Extraordinary Measures

sections.content: Extraordinary Measures (2010) represents a pivotal moment in medical drama storytelling, following the real-life crusade of John Crowley (Brendan Fraser) to save his children from Pompe disease. The film shares DNA with other pharmaceutical-focused dramas like Lorenzo's Oil (1992) and Dallas Buyers Club (2013), but uniquely focuses on the business side of drug development. Harrison Ford's portrayal of Dr. Robert Stonehill captures the friction between academic research and commercial medicine, while highlighting how personal stakes drive scientific innovation.

sections.content: The film fits into a larger tradition of medical breakthrough narratives, though it takes a different approach from more research-focused films like Awakenings (1990) or The Constant Gardener (2005). Where those films emphasize clinical trials or pharmaceutical conspiracies, Extraordinary Measures spotlights the entrepreneurial drive needed to push medical research forward. The story's emphasis on fundraising and corporate politics offers a rare glimpse into how life-saving treatments actually make it to market.

Fraser's performance marked an important shift in his career, moving from comedy and action roles to more dramatic territory. His portrayal of a desperate father shares emotional DNA with films like John Q (2002), where parents confront broken medical systems to save their children. The film also builds on themes explored in Miss Evers' Boys (1997), examining how personal ethics intersect with medical research. SUBHEAD: Medical Ethics and Corporate Reality

sections.content: While many medical dramas focus on doctor-patient relationships or miracle cures, Extraordinary Measures delves into the complex reality of bringing new drugs to market. Like Side Effects (2013) and The Constant Gardener (2005), it exposes the tangled web of corporate interests, academic research, and FDA regulations. Harrison Ford's Dr. Stonehill embodies the brilliant but difficult researcher archetype seen in films like A Beautiful Mind (2001), highlighting how genius often clashes with institutional constraints.
